Homework 7 - Random Walk and Security Simulation

08 Nov 2025

Introduction to Random Walks and Symmetric Binary Processes

While Homework 4 explored the Law of Large Numbers through one-directional accumulation (counting successes from 0 to n), Homework 7 introduces a fundamentally different perspective: the symmetric random walk. Instead of tracking cumulative success rates, we now model a process where each step can move us either up (+1, secure) or down (-1, breached), creating trajectories that can reach both positive and negative scores.

This homework demonstrates how a simple security model—a server facing weekly attacks—naturally leads to one of the most important structures in probability theory and combinatorics: the random walk and its connection to binomial distributions.

Problem Statement

Server Security Scenario

Consider a server that receives security updates every week for n weeks. There are m attackers who attempt to breach the system, with each attacker having an independent probability p of successfully penetrating the server in any given week.

Scoring System:

  • If the server remains secure in week i: add +1 to the cumulative score
  • If the server is breached in week i: add -1 to the cumulative score

Starting from score 0, after n weeks the cumulative score S(n) can range from -n (breached every week) to +n (secure every week).

Mathematical Formulation

Let Xᵢ be the outcome of week i:

Xᵢ = +1  with probability q = P(server secure) = (1-p)^m
Xᵢ = -1  with probability p' = P(server breached) = 1-(1-p)^m

The cumulative score after n weeks:

S(n) = X₁ + X₂ + ... + Xₙ

where S(n) ∈ {-n, -n+2, -n+4, …, n-2, n}.

Note: S(n) can only reach values with the same parity as n (both even or both odd).

Theoretical Background

Random Walk vs Bernoulli Process

Aspect Homework 4 (Bernoulli) Homework 7 (Random Walk)
Step values 0 or 1 -1 or +1
Range [0, n] [-n, +n]
Direction One-way accumulation Bidirectional movement
Final position k ∈ {0,1,…,n} s ∈ {-n,-n+2,…,n}
Path count to k C(n,k) C(n,(n+s)/2)
Distribution Binomial(n,p) Transformed Binomial
Application Success counting Position tracking

The Fundamental Relationship

If we have k secure weeks (+1) and (n-k) breached weeks (-1), the final score is:

S(n) = k - (n-k) = 2k - n

Therefore:

k = (n + S(n)) / 2

This means:

  • Score s = +n ⟹ k = n (all secure)
  • Score s = 0 ⟹ k = n/2 (equal secure/breach)
  • Score s = -n ⟹ k = 0 (all breached)

Number of Trajectories

The number of trajectories reaching score s after n steps is:

N(n, s) = C(n, k) = C(n, (n+s)/2)

where C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!) is the binomial coefficient.

Total trajectories: 2ⁿ (each week: secure or breach)

Pascal’s Triangle Connection

The trajectory counts form Pascal’s triangle:

                    1                        n=0
                  1   1                      n=1
                1   2   1                    n=2
              1   3   3   1                  n=3
            1   4   6   4   1                n=4
          1   5  10  10   5   1              n=5

For random walk, we read the same triangle but map positions differently:

  • n=4: scores {-4, -2, 0, 2, 4} have counts {1, 4, 6, 4, 1}
  • n=5: scores {-5, -3, -1, 1, 3, 5} have counts {1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1}

Recurrence Relation

The number of paths satisfies:

N(n, s) = N(n-1, s-1) + N(n-1, s+1)

This is the same recurrence as Pascal’s triangle:

C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k)

Interpretation: To reach position s at step n, we must have been at s-1 or s+1 at step n-1.

Methodology

Simulation Parameters

  • n: Number of weeks (steps): 10, 50, 100, 500
  • m: Number of attackers: 1-10
  • p: Individual attacker success probability: 0.1, 0.3, 0.5
  • trajectories: Number of simulation runs: 100-1000

Probability Calculation

For m independent attackers, each with probability p of success:

q = P(all m attackers fail) = (1-p)^m
p' = P(at least one succeeds) = 1-(1-p)^m

Examples:

  • m=1, p=0.3: q=0.7, p’=0.3
  • m=2, p=0.3: q=0.49, p’=0.51
  • m=5, p=0.3: q=0.168, p’=0.832

Implementation Strategy

  1. Generate Random Walk: For each trajectory, simulate n weeks where each week results in +1 (secure) or -1 (breached)

  2. Track Cumulative Score: Maintain running sum S(t) for t=1,2,…,n

  3. Count Final Positions: Tally how many trajectories end at each possible score s ∈ {-n, -n+2, …, n-2, n}

  4. Compare with Theory: Compare empirical counts with theoretical C(n, (n+s)/2)

  5. Visualization:

    • Plot all trajectories as paths through (step, score) space
    • Show histogram of final scores
    • Overlay theoretical binomial distribution
    • Display Pascal’s triangle structure

Results and Analysis

Example 1: Balanced Security (p = 0.5, m = 1)

With one attacker having 50% success rate:

  • q = 0.5 (secure)
  • p’ = 0.5 (breached)

This creates a symmetric random walk.

Figure 1: Simulation of 1000 random walk trajectories with p_secure = 0.5 (symmetric walk) over 50 weeks. Left: All trajectories starting from score 0. Right: Distribution of final scores showing concentration around 0.

Simulation: n=20 weeks, 1000 trajectories

Final score distribution:

  • Most trajectories cluster around 0
  • Follows binomial(20, 0.5) transformed to random walk scores
  • Maximum at score 0 (equal secure/breach weeks)

Theoretical counts (from Pascal’s triangle, row 20):

Score:  -20  -18  -16  -14  -12  -10   -8   -6   -4   -2    0 ...
Count:    1   20  190  1140 4845 15504 38760 77520 125970 167960 184756 ...

Example 2: Secure System (p = 0.2, m = 1)

One attacker with 20% success rate:

  • q = 0.8 (secure)
  • p’ = 0.2 (breached)

Asymmetric random walk with drift toward positive scores.

Figure 2: Simulation with p_secure = 0.8 showing asymmetric random walk with positive drift. Most trajectories end in positive territory.

Expected final score:

E[S(n)] = n(q - p') = 20(0.8 - 0.2) = 12

Distribution shifts right—most trajectories end in positive territory.

Example 3: Multiple Attackers (m = 5, p = 0.3)

Five attackers, each with 30% success:

q = (1-0.3)^5 = 0.168
p' = 1 - 0.168 = 0.832

System is breached 83.2% of weeks—strong negative drift.

Figure 3: Five attackers scenario with strong negative drift (p_secure = 0.168). Trajectories predominantly end in negative scores.

Expected final score:

E[S(n)] = n(0.168 - 0.832) = -13.3 (for n=20)

Most trajectories end far in negative territory.

Convergence Analysis

As n increases, the distribution becomes:

  1. More concentrated (relative to range)
  2. Approximately normal (Central Limit Theorem)
  3. Better matched to theoretical predictions

Standard deviation of final score:

σ = √(n · 4qp') = 2√(nqp')

For n=100, q=0.5:

σ = 2√(100 · 0.5 · 0.5) = 10

Mathematical Connections

1. Binomial Coefficients

Number of paths to score s:

N(n, s) = C(n, (n+s)/2) = n! / [((n+s)/2)! · ((n-s)/2)!]

2. Pascal’s Triangle Identity

C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k)

In random walk terms:

N(n, s) = N(n-1, s-1) + N(n-1, s+1)

Figure 7: Pascal’s Triangle visualization showing how binomial coefficients represent the number of paths to each position in the random walk.

3. Binomial Expansion

(A + B)^n = Σ C(n,k) A^k B^(n-k)

Setting A = B = 1:

2^n = Σ C(n,k)  (total number of trajectories)

4. Symmetry

For symmetric random walk (q = p’ = 0.5):

N(n, s) = N(n, -s)

This reflects Pascal’s triangle symmetry: C(n,k) = C(n, n-k)

5. Fibonacci Connection

Though not directly visible, Fibonacci numbers appear in diagonal sums of Pascal’s triangle:

F(n) = C(n,0) + C(n-1,1) + C(n-2,2) + ...

Conclusion

This homework demonstrates that random walks naturally emerge from symmetric binary processes and connect deeply to fundamental combinatorial structures. Key insights:

  1. Dual Interpretation: The same binomial coefficients count both:
    • Paths in random walk reaching position s
    • Ways to choose k successes from n trials

  2. Pascal’s Triangle: Provides trajectory counts through simple recursive structure

  3. Distribution Convergence: As n,m increase, empirical counts approach theoretical predictions

  4. Practical Application: Server security modeling illustrates real-world random walk behavior

  5. Mathematical Beauty: Random walks unite probability, combinatorics, and number theory

The transition from Homework 4’s one-directional accumulation to this homework’s bidirectional movement reveals the rich structure underlying stochastic processes.
